title: Can every two-way NFA be determinized with polynomially many states?
formal: Do universal constants C,k≥1 exist such that, for every n≥1, every finite nonempty input alphabet Σ and every two-way nondeterministic finite automaton A over Σ with at most n states, there is a two-way deterministic finite automaton D over the same alphabet with at most C(n+1)^k states satisfying L(D)=L(A)? Equivalence must hold on all finite input words, without a length bound.
definitions: The read-only input tape contains a left endmarker, a word w∈Σ*, and a right endmarker. Each automaton has one head, initially on the left endmarker, a finite set Q of states with a designated initial state and designated halting accepting states. In each nonhalting configuration it uses its current state and the scanned symbol to choose a new state and a head displacement in {−1,0,+1}; moves outside the endmarkers are forbidden. A missing transition rejects that branch. A word is accepted if some finite computation reaches an accepting state. Infinite nonaccepting branches do not count as acceptance. For a deterministic automaton there is at most one available transition in each state-symbol pair, and its unique infinite run, if any, rejects. There is no work tape, rewritable input, second head, stack, counter, randomness or advice. State count includes all control and halting states, but the bound is independent of word length and alphabet size. The target is existence of D for each A; computing D from A is not required to take polynomial time. Standard endmarker and stay-put conventions change these state bounds only by polynomial factors.
answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
context:
All four basic finite-automaton models—one-way or two-way, deterministic or nondeterministic—recognize exactly the regular languages. Their descriptions can nevertheless have very different sizes. The familiar subset construction gives an exponential conversion from a one-way NFA to a one-way DFA. The open issue is whether the deterministic machine can avoid that cost by repeatedly revisiting the original input instead of remembering all possible nondeterministic states at once.

A simple example shows why a one-way lower bound is insufficient. Over {0,1}, consider words whose r-th symbol from the right is 1. A one-way deterministic automaton must distinguish all binary suffixes of length r and therefore needs at least 2^r states. A two-way deterministic automaton can scan to the right endmarker, walk left r positions while counting in its finite control, and inspect the symbol. It uses O(r) states. Rereading changes the representation cost even though the accepted language is unchanged.

Known unrestricted upper bounds still pass through a one-way representation and are exponential in a polynomial of the number of states. At the opposite end, exponential separations are known if the deterministic target has restricted head motion, such as reversing only at endmarkers. Those restrictions can themselves make deterministic automata exponentially larger. A lower bound using them therefore cannot be transferred to an unrestricted 2DFA without another argument.

The unary case remains meaningful: the input then consists of repetitions of one letter, and only its length can carry information. Unary two-way NFAs can be simulated by two-way DFAs with n^{O(log n)} states. This is far smaller than an exponential bound but still exceeds every fixed polynomial. It demonstrates that even removing almost all input syntax does not make the remaining determinization question routine.

Connections to logarithmic-space computation require careful quantifiers. Kapoutsis proves that polynomial-state deterministic simulation on inputs of length at most the source state count is equivalent to NL⊆L/poly. Here L/poly allows a deterministic logarithmic-space machine polynomially long advice depending only on input length. That theorem concerns bounded-length agreement, whereas this card requires agreement on every word. It should not be restated as an unconditional equivalence of the full Sakoda–Sipser question with L=NL.

Clerici Lorenzini, Pighizzini, and Prigioniero study letter-bounded languages in 2025: languages contained in a_1*⋯a_t* for fixed letters. They obtain a polynomial-cost normal form in which nondeterministic choices and head reversals occur at endmarkers. The source language restriction is crucial; the theorem does not put every two-way NFA into that normal form.

Guillon, Prigioniero, and Taheri’s STACS 2026 theorem complements arbitrary two-way NFAs with a polynomial-size self-verifying 1-limited automaton. Such a machine can annotate input cells on their first visit; the construction uses a shared guessed annotation that subsequent traversals can inspect. It remains a recognizer of regular languages, but its ability to retain those annotations is absent from a 2DFA. Their introduction explicitly leaves ordinary determinization and ordinary two-way-NFA complementation open.
why: A principal unresolved measure of the succinctness provided by nondeterminism. It isolates the issue in finite-state machines, connects to nonuniform space complexity, and asks whether revisiting read-only data can replace a large internal record of possible computations.

importance.reason: The flagship state-complexity problem for two-way finite automata, open since 1978, with unusually direct connections between finite-state descriptions and logarithmic-space complexity.

progress.text: Sakoda and Sipser formulate the polynomial-state simulation questions and conjecture that nondeterminism cannot always be removed with polynomial cost.
The Geffert–Mereghetti–Pighizzini simulation gives n^{O(log n)} states for unary two-way NFAs. It leaves a polynomial-versus-superpolynomial gap.
Kapoutsis characterizes polynomial-state simulation on short inputs by NL⊆L/poly, carefully distinguishing input-length restrictions and advice.
Clerici Lorenzini and coauthors obtain a polynomial-size normal form for two-way NFAs accepting letter-bounded languages.
Guillon and coauthors give polynomial-size complementation using self-verifying 1-limited automata, with rewritable annotations; the unrestricted read-only determinization question remains open.

status_note: Checked through 10 September 2026. STACS 2026 explicitly retains the ordinary two-way determinization problem as open. The new complementation theorem uses a stronger target with writable annotations. This card permits unrestricted head motion but only one head and a read-only tape, and requires equivalence on words of every length.

sentences: Two-way finite automata can reread their input by moving their head in either direction.
This project asks whether every n-state nondeterministic machine has an equivalent deterministic two-way machine with polynomially many states.
Both machines must agree on all finite words, with no restriction on input length.
Rereading sometimes replaces exponentially much one-way memory, but that observation does not supply a general simulation.
Resolving the question would quantify how much finite-state succinctness comes from nondeterministic choice once unrestricted revisiting of the input is available.
